title: Chapter 83 — Jonah Historically Regarded
paragraphs: The last chapter mentioned the historical story of Jonah and the whale. Now, some Nantucketers are rather suspicious of this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then, there were some skeptical Greeks and Romans who broke ranks with the orthodox pagans of their day and doubted, just as much, the story of Hercules and the whale and that of Arion and the dolphin; and yet their doubts did not make those traditions the slightest bit less factual, for all that.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman's chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this. He had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles decorated with curious, unscientific engravings, one of which showed Jonah's whale with two spouts in his head — a peculiarity true only of one species of Leviathan (the Right Whale and the varieties of that order), of which the fishermen have this saying: "A penny roll would choke him"; his swallow is so very small. But Bishop Jebb has an answer to this ready in advance. It is not necessary, the Bishop hints, to think of Jonah as entombed in the whale's belly, but rather as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough of the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale's mouth would hold a couple of whist-tables and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have tucked himself away in a hollow tooth; but, on second thought, the Right Whale has no teeth.

Another reason Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) gave for his lack of faith in this matter of the prophet was something vaguely to do with the imprisoned body and the whale's gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German biblical interpreter supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a whale that was already dead — just as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents and crawled inside them. Besides, other continental commentators have guessed that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he promptly escaped to another vessel close by, some vessel with a whale for a figurehead; and, I would add, possibly called "The Whale," just as some craft nowadays are christened the "Shark," the "Gull," or the "Eagle." Nor has there been any shortage of learned interpreters who have held that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah simply meant a life-preserver — an inflated bag of wind — which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery death. Poor Sag-Harbor, then, seems beaten on every side. But he had still another reason for his lack of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days' journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, which is very much more than three days' journey from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet that close to Nineveh? There was. He could have carried him around by way of the Cape of Good Hope. But leaving aside the voyage through the whole length of the Mediterranean and another up the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, such a theory would mean sailing right around Africa in three days — to say nothing of the fact that the Tigris, near where Nineveh stood, is too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, the idea of Jonah rounding the Cape of Good Hope at such an early date would rob Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, of the honor of finding that great headland, and so make modern history a liar.

But all these foolish arguments of old Sag-Harbor only showed his foolish pride of reason — a thing all the more blameworthy in him, since he had little learning beyond what he had picked up from the sun and the sea. I say it only shows his foolish, impious pride, and his abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy. For a Portuguese Catholic priest put forward this very idea of Jonah's going to Nineveh by way of the Cape of Good Hope as a remarkable magnifying of the general miracle. And so it was. Besides, to this day the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveler in old Harris's Voyages tells of a Turkish mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which there was a miraculous lamp that burned without any oil.
